LEAD-BASED PAINT DISCLOSURE
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Alex Lee

CERTIFICATION AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF DISCLOSURE
Seller's/Landlord's Disclosure (initial one):

___ Known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards are present in the housing at 123 Main St, Springfield, described as follows: ______________________________

___ Acme Properties, LLC has no knowledge of lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the housing.

Records and Reports available to Acme Properties, LLC pertaining to lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the housing (list documents below, or state "None available"):

______________________________________________________

Buyer's/Tenant's Acknowledgment (initial each):

___ Jordan Alex Lee has received the information and records/reports identified above.

___ Jordan Alex Lee has received the EPA-approved pamphlet, Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home.

___ (Sale transactions only) Jordan Alex Lee has received a 10-day opportunity (or a mutually agreed alternative period, if any: ______) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for lead-based paint hazards before becoming obligated under the contract, or has waived that opportunity in writing.

Agent's Acknowledgment (if an agent is involved in the transaction):

___ The agent has informed Acme Properties, LLC of Acme Properties, LLC's obligations under 42 U.S.C. § 4852d and is aware of the agent's own duty to ensure compliance with those requirements.

Signed:

Seller/Landlord: Acme Properties, LLC _______________________ Date: _______________
Buyer/Tenant: Jordan Alex Lee _______________________ Date: _______________
Agent (if any): _______________________ Date: _______________

TARGET HOUSING AND REGULATORY EXEMPTIONS (LEAD-BASED PAINT)
The federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement applies to "target housing" — any housing constructed prior to 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities, or any 0-bedroom dwelling, unless a child under 6 resides or is expected to reside there (in a jurisdiction that banned lead-based paint before 1978, HUD's Secretary may designate an earlier cutoff date at the Secretary's discretion). Separately, the implementing regulation excludes four categories of transaction from the disclosure subpart entirely, even where the housing would otherwise be "target housing": sales of target housing at foreclosure; leases of housing found lead-based-paint-free by a certified inspector; short-term leases of 100 days or less where no renewal or extension can occur; and renewals of an existing lease where the lessor already made the required disclosures and no new information has come into the lessor's possession.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The term “target housing” means any housing constructed prior to 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities or any 0-bedroom dwelling (unless any child who is less than 6 years of age resides or is expected to reside in such housing). In the case of jurisdictions which banned the sale or use of lead-based paint prior to 1978, the Secretary, at the Secretary’s discretion, may designate an earlier date."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 4851b(27), Federal law, definition of "target housing" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4851b)
  "This subpart applies to all transactions to sell or lease target housing, including subleases, with the exception of the following: (a) Sales of target housing at foreclosure."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.101(a), Federal regulation, foreclosure-sale exemption (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.101)
  "(b) Leases of target housing that have been found to be lead-based paint free by an inspector certified under the Federal certification program or under a federally accredited State or tribal certification program."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.101(b), Federal regulation, certified lead-free lease exemption (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.101)
  "(c) Short-term leases of 100 days or less, where no lease renewal or extension can occur."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.101(c), Federal regulation, short-term-lease exemption (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.101)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how target housing and its exemptions are defined nationwide — not a claim that every property or transaction is covered, since these exemptions apply on their own terms and a specific property's or transaction's classification isn't resolved by this document. Three of the citations below (40 C.F.R. § 745.101(a), (b), and (c)) are subsections of the same regulatory section; the statutory definition (a separate U.S. Code section) is an independently authored source. Separately, the statute and the EPA regulation place the "(unless any child... resides)" parenthetical immediately after "0-bedroom dwelling," while HUD's parallel regulation (24 C.F.R. § 35.86) places the identical parenthetical immediately after "housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities" instead — a genuine wording difference between the two agencies' codifications of the same joint rule that this document doesn't resolve.

LEAD HAZARD DISCLOSURE DUTIES (SALE OR LEASE)
Before a purchaser or lessee of target housing becomes obligated under a contract to purchase or lease, the seller or lessor must provide the purchaser or lessee an EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet — such as the EPA document "Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home" (EPA #747-K-94-001) or an equivalent pamphlet approved for use in that state; disclose the presence of any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards, along with any additional information available (such as the basis for the determination, the location of the paint or hazard, and the condition of painted surfaces); and provide any records or reports available concerning lead-based paint or hazards, including records regarding common areas. The seller or lessor must make the same known-hazard and records disclosure to any agent involved in the transaction. If any required disclosure activity happens after the purchaser or lessee has already made an offer, the seller or lessor must complete it before accepting that offer and allow the purchaser or lessee an opportunity to review the information and possibly amend the offer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The regulations shall require that, before the purchaser or lessee is obligated under any contract to purchase or lease the housing, the seller or lessor shall— (A) provide the purchaser or lessee with a lead hazard information pamphlet, as prescribed by the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency under section 406 of the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2686]; (B) disclose to the purchaser or lessee the presence of any known lead-based paint, or any known lead-based paint hazards, in such housing and provide to the purchaser or lessee any lead hazard evaluation report available to the seller or lessor; and (C) permit the purchaser a 10-day period (unless the parties mutually agree upon a different period of time) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint hazards."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(1), Federal law, pamphlet/disclosure/records requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4852d)
  "The seller or lessor shall provide the purchaser or lessee with an EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet. Such pamphlets include the EPA document entitled Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home (EPA #747-K-94-001) or an equivalent pamphlet that has been approved for use in that State by EPA."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.107(a)(1), Federal regulation, EPA-approved pamphlet requirement (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.107)
  "The seller or lessor shall disclose to the purchaser or lessee the presence of any known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the target housing being sold or leased. The seller or lessor shall also disclose any additional information available concerning the known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards, such as the basis for the determination that lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards exist, the location of the lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards, and the condition of the painted surfaces."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.107(a)(2), Federal regulation, known-hazard disclosure requirement (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.107)
  "If any of the disclosure activities identified in paragraph (a) of this section occurs after the purchaser or lessee has provided an offer to purchase or lease the housing, the seller or lessor shall complete the required disclosure activities prior to accepting the purchaser's or lessee's offer and allow the purchaser or lessee an opportunity to review the information and possibly amend the offer."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.107(b), Federal regulation, post-offer disclosure timing (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.107)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the disclosure duties that apply nationwide to a sale or lease of target housing — not a claim that every property or transaction is covered, since target-housing exemptions apply. Three of the citations below (40 C.F.R. § 745.107(a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)) are subsections of the same regulatory section; the statutory citation (42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(1)) is the independently authored source the regulation implements.

TEN-DAY INSPECTION OPPORTUNITY (SALE TRANSACTIONS ONLY)
For a purchase (as distinct from a lease) of target housing, before the purchaser becomes obligated under the contract, the seller must permit the purchaser a 10-day period — unless the parties mutually agree in writing to a different period — to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for lead-based paint hazards; the purchaser may waive this opportunity by so indicating in writing. Every contract for the purchase and sale of an interest in target housing must contain a Lead Warning Statement and a statement signed by the purchaser confirming having read and understood the Lead Warning Statement, received the pamphlet, and either had the 10-day (or agreed) opportunity or waived it. By its own terms, this inspection-opportunity requirement runs to a "purchaser," not a "lessee" — the parallel disclosure duties that apply to a lease do not include a counterpart risk-assessment or inspection-opportunity provision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Regulations promulgated under this section shall provide that every contract for the purchase and sale of any interest in target housing shall contain a Lead Warning Statement and a statement signed by the purchaser that the purchaser has— (A) read the Lead Warning Statement and understands its contents; (B) received a lead hazard information pamphlet; and (C) had a 10-day opportunity (unless the parties mutually agreed upon a different period of time) before becoming obligated under the contract to purchase the housing to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint hazards."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(2), Federal law, purchase-contract certification requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4852d)
  "Before a purchaser is obligated under any contract to purchase target housing, the seller shall permit the purchaser a 10-day period (unless the parties mutually agree, in writing, upon a different period of time) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.110(a), Federal regulation, the 10-day opportunity (purchaser only) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.110)
  "Not withstanding paragraph (a) of this section, a purchaser may waive the opportunity to conduct the risk assessment or inspection by so indicating in writing."
  — 40 C.F.R. § 745.110(b), Federal regulation, written waiver (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-R/part-745/subpart-F/section-745.110)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a requirement that, on its face, applies to a purchase and not to a lease of target housing — not a claim about how a specific transaction is or should be structured. The two regulatory citations below (40 C.F.R. § 745.110(a) and (b)) are subsections of the same regulatory section; the statutory citation (42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(2)) is the independently authored source the regulation implements.

CIVIL PENALTIES AND PRIVATE LIABILITY FOR LEAD DISCLOSURE VIOLATIONS
A knowing violation of the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement carries several distinct consequences. It exposes the violator to civil money penalties under a separate cross-referenced HUD penalty statute, and HUD's Secretary is authorized to seek an injunction against any violation in federal district court. Independently of any government enforcement action, a person who knowingly violates the disclosure requirement is jointly and severally liable to the purchaser or lessee for treble damages — three times the amount of the damages the purchaser or lessee incurred — and a court may award the prevailing plaintiff court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and expert witness fees in a suit for those damages. Failing or refusing to comply is also a prohibited act under the Toxic Substances Control Act, subjecting the violator to a civil penalty of not more than $10,000 per violation under that Act's separate enforcement provisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Any person who knowingly violates any provision of this section shall be subject to civil money penalties in accordance with the provisions of section 3545 of this title."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(b)(1), Federal law, HUD civil money penalty cross-reference (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4852d)
  "Any person who knowingly violates the provisions of this section shall be jointly and severally liable to the purchaser or lessee in an amount equal to 3 times the amount of damages incurred by such individual."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(b)(3), Federal law, treble-damages private civil liability (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4852d)
  "It shall be a prohibited act under section 409 of the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2689] for any person to fail or refuse to comply with a provision of this section or with any rule or order issued under this section. For purposes of enforcing this section under the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2601 et seq.], the penalty for each violation applicable under section 16 of that Act [15 U.S.C. 2615] shall not be more than $10,000."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(b)(5), Federal law, TSCA prohibited-act enforcement and penalty cap (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4852d)
  "Any person who knowingly violates the provisions of this subpart shall be jointly and severally liable to the purchaser or lessee in an amount equal to 3 times the amount of damages incurred by such individual."
  — 24 C.F.R. § 35.96(c), Federal regulation (HUD), parallel treble-damages codification (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-A/part-35/subpart-A/section-35.96)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that this federal disclosure duty carries enforcement teeth — both a private damages remedy and government penalty authority — not a claim about what penalty a specific violation would draw, since that depends on facts (knowledge, actual damages, and how a court or agency exercises its discretion) this document doesn't resolve. Three of the citations below (42 U.S.C. § 4852d(b)(1), (b)(3), and (b)(5)) are subsections of the same statutory section; the regulatory citation (24 C.F.R. § 35.96(c)) is HUD's independently codified restatement of the treble-damages rule. One correction worth flagging: the treble-damages private-liability provision is at § 4852d(b)(3), not (b)(5) — (b)(5) is instead the provision making noncompliance a "prohibited act" enforceable under the Toxic Substances Control Act's separate, capped civil-penalty scheme; the two are easy to conflate but are legally distinct remedies. This document also does not independently verify the substance of 42 U.S.C. § 3545 (the cross-referenced HUD civil-penalty statute) or its current penalty amounts, which weren't part of this research pass.

REQUIRED LEAD WARNING STATEMENT (SALE AND LEASE VERSIONS)
For the sale of 123 Main St, Springfield, the following Lead Warning Statement is the exact statutorily and regulatorily required text for a purchase-and-sale contract, printed in large type on a separate attached sheet:

"Every purchaser of any interest in residential real property on which a residential dwelling was built prior to 1978 is notified that such property may present exposure to lead from lead-based paint that may place young children at risk of developing lead poisoning. Lead poisoning in young children may produce permanent neurological damage, including learning disabilities, reduced intelligence quotient, behavioral problems, and impaired memory. Lead poisoning also poses a particular risk to pregnant women. The seller of any interest in residential real property is required to provide the buyer with any information on lead-based paint hazards from risk assessments or inspections in the seller's possession and notify the buyer of any known lead-based paint hazards. A risk assessment or inspection for possible lead-based paint hazards is recommended prior to purchase."

For the lease of 123 Main St, Springfield, the following is the separate, shorter Lead Warning Statement the regulation prescribes for a lease contract:

"Housing built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint. Lead from paint, paint chips, and dust can pose health hazards if not managed properly. Lead exposure is especially harmful to young children and pregnant women. Before renting pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose the presence of known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling. Lessees must also receive a federally approved pamphlet on lead poisoning prevention."

Only the version matching the actual transaction type — sale or lease — applies to a given transaction; the two are not interchangeable.
